analysis: scripts/install.sh adds DARKBLOOM_PRERELEASE_DESIGNATED_REQUIREMENT (`identifier "io.darkbloom.provider"`, head lines 37 and 63-70). select_provider_identity picks it when the release-JSON VERSION contains `-dev.` or `-staging.`. VERSION is attacker-influenceable by whoever controls the release record or release-registration key (A-005); the installer does not check COORD_URL against an allow-list or PRODUCTION_COORD_URL. This removes the Apple anchor/team-OU pin that was independent of the bundle hash, which comes from the same JSON. Staging maps to the production identity and paths (~/.darkbloom), so a relaxed-signature build can overwrite the production install. The fan-helper requirement is unchanged and still pinned, but only if the bundle includes the helper. verify_staged_app also executes the staged binary (`runtime-smoke`) before commit, now even when unsigned. The test changes (scripts/test-install-identity.py) model ad-hoc signatures. They assert that prod rejects ad-hoc signatures, but they do not test a prod COORD_URL combined with a -dev or -staging version, which is the exploitable case. Threat-model note: TB-009 and T-034 should record that installer trust now depends on a server-supplied version marker. The platform-served byte-for-byte snapshot in darkbloom-platform must be coordinated.

findings.detail: select_provider_identity now chooses the relaxed requirement `identifier "io.darkbloom.provider"` whenever VERSION contains `-dev.` or `-staging.`. VERSION is parsed from the same /v1/releases/latest response that supplies url, bundle_hash, binary_hash and metallib_hash. The installer never checks that COORD_URL is a dev or staging coordinator, and it does not compare it with PRODUCTION_COORD_URL. The comment 'a prod coordinator is never served a pre-release version' is a server-side assumption, not an installer check. Previously the Apple-anchor/team-OU pin on the staged app was the independent control. It held even if the release record, bundle URL, bundle hash or binary hash were attacker-controlled. Now anyone who can alter or poison the release record can bypass it. Examples are a compromised release-registration key (A-005), a bad registry entry, or a hostile coordinator for a non-production COORD_URL. The attacker sets version to something like `9.9.9-dev.1` or `9.9.9-staging.1` and ships a self-signed or ad-hoc bundle that carries the right bundle identifier and a matching hash. The installer accepts it and runs `runtime-smoke` from it. The install is then committed and the app handles consumer plaintext and the provider keys. Fix: apply the relaxed requirement only when COORD_URL is an explicitly allow-listed non-production host. Production-built installers should keep the full Apple-team requirement unconditionally. Alternatively, gate the relaxation behind an explicit opt-in flag or environment variable that is not derived from server-supplied data.
findings.title: Installer drops the Apple Developer ID anchor based on an untrusted version string from the release JSON

findings.detail: The new `-staging.` marker relaxes the signature requirement. However, identity selection still maps only `-dev.` to the separate `darkbloom-dev` identity and path. A `-staging.` version falls into the default branch: CLI_NAME=darkbloom, APP_NAME=Darkbloom.app and INSTALL_DIR=~/.darkbloom. A self-signed or ad-hoc staging build therefore replaces the production app via commit_staged_app. It also repoints the /usr/local/bin and PATH symlinks and writes the staging coordinator into the production provider.toml. This breaks the stated isolation property at lines 42-45 for staging. It also means one weakened-signature artifact installs directly into the production identity and keychain access-group context. Fix: give staging its own identity and paths, or refuse relaxed-signature installs that would target the production identity.
findings.title: Staging pre-release builds share the production identity and install path, so a relaxed-signature build overwrites the production install
